title: A one minute pose was said to change your hormones.
description:
A one minute pose was said to change your hormones. Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported higher testosterone and lower cortisol after a high power pose.

The final sample of the original study, after five exclusions.

A larger replication found no hormone effect. Ranehill and colleagues used 200 people, 98 women and 102 men, and held the poses for three minutes. Testosterone, cortisol and risk taking did not change significantly.

People still said they felt more powerful. That self reported feeling was the one result the replication confirmed.

The lead author of the 2010 study. She said she does not believe the power pose effects are real, and listed flaws including checking the result while running the study in batches.

The feeling held up. The hormone claim did not.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_posing (read): established that Carney, Cuddy and Yap published the original study in Psychological Science in 2010 with 42 participants, reporting higher testosterone and lower cortisol; that the 2015 Ranehill replication used a larger sample and confirmed felt power but found no physiological or behavioural effects; and that Carney publicly stated she does not believe the effects are real.
- http://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/dana_carney/pdf_My%20position%20on%20power%20poses.pdf (read): Carney's own statement. Established that the final sample was N = 42 after 5 exclusions, that subjects were run in batches while the effect was checked, and that she says she does not believe the power pose effects are real.
- https://www.zne.uzh.ch/dam/jcr:e5fc4c3c-d50e-4aa9-96ab-4389e426d20d/Psychological%20Science-2015-Ranehill-0956797614553946.pdf (read): the replication paper. Established N = 200 (98 women, 102 men), poses held for 3 minutes where the original used 1, a significant effect on self reported feelings of power, and no significant effect on testosterone, cortisol or risk taking.
